title: Artificial intelligence across the gastric cancer care continuum: Clinical evidence, multimodal integration, and translation

license.text: This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/4.0/).

paragraphs.en: Gastric cancer continues to impose a substantial global burden despite declining age-standardized incidence and mortality rates in some regions.1 According to Global Cancer Observatory (GLOBOCAN) 2022, stomach cancer accounted for more than 968,000 new cases and nearly 660,000 deaths worldwide,2 underscoring its status as one of the deadliest common malignancies.2 The burden remains especially high in East Asia, where organized screening programs and high procedural volumes have made early detection a central clinical priority.3 Nevertheless, many patients are still diagnosed at locally advanced or metastatic stages.4 Early lesions may be endoscopically subtle, symptoms are often nonspecific, and the disease exhibits marked histologic, molecular, and spatial heterogeneities. Gastric cancer is, therefore, not only a high-burden disease but also one that is highly prone to error across the clinical pathway.5

These clinical challenges align closely with the strengths of modern artificial intelligence (AI).5 Over the past decade, the field has progressed from conventional machine learning models based on limited structured variables to deep neural networks capable of analyzing high-dimensional image data.5 More recently, the field has moved toward multimodal and foundation model paradigms that learn transferable representations from large, weakly labeled, or unlabeled datasets.6 In gastric cancer, this transition is especially consequential because management depends on integrating heterogeneous data streams, including white-light and image-enhanced endoscopy, computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT), histopathology, immunophenotyping, molecular testing, laboratory findings, and treatment trajectories.7 Few solid tumors illustrate the need for cross-modal clinical AI as clearly as gastric cancer.8

Recent reviews suggest that gastric cancer is emerging as one of the most active areas in gastrointestinal oncology for AI translation.9 A 2024 systematic review focused on gastric adenocarcinoma synthesized studies from PubMed, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library and concluded that AI is already reshaping the diagnostic and management pathways.10 A 2023 systematic review of AI-assisted endoscopy identified 42 original studies and found that deep learning models frequently matched or outperformed endoscopists in tasks related to early gastric neoplasia.11 The central question is no longer whether AI can recognize patterns in gastric cancer, but whether it can improve real-world decision-making as a trustworthy, equitable, and workflow integrated tool.12

The present review, therefore, adopts a clinically oriented and translational perspective. Its distinct contribution is to examine AI across the complete gastric cancer care continuum, while explicitly comparing evidence maturity, clinical actionability, workflow compatibility, and regional transportability. It distinguishes near-term deployable systems, including real-time endoscopy and routine-slide pathology, from discovery-oriented technologies such as single-cell analysis, spatial transcriptomics, foundation models, and digital twins. Particular attention is given to multimodal integration, cross-regional generalization, clinician-AI interaction, regulatory governance, and medico-legal responsibility.13

The scope includes AI applications in prevention and risk stratification, endoscopic detection and characterization, CT and PET/CT staging, digital pathology and biomarker prescreening, prognostic modeling, treatment-response prediction, surgical support, and longitudinal decision support. Four questions guide this review. Which applications currently have the strongest clinical evidence? How do imaging, pathology, multimodal, and omics-based approaches add value beyond endoscopic AI? Which methodological and geographic barriers limit reproducibility and equitable deployment? What validation, workflow, regulatory, and governance requirements are necessary before these systems can improve patient care? (Figure 1).

This article was designed as a structured narrative review addressing the clinical and translational development of AI in gastric cancer. The narrative approach was selected because the evidence spans heterogeneous clinical tasks, data modalities, model architectures, outcome definitions, and study designs that are not suitable for a single pooled quantitative analysis. The conduct and reporting of the review were informed by the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA).

This review was not prospectively registered and not designed as a formal systematic review. Accordingly, it does not claim full compliance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses. Transparency was instead strengthened through a reproducible search description, explicit eligibility criteria, structured evidence characterization, and an adapted study-identification framework presented.

PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection were searched for relevant studies published from January 1, 2022 through July 2026. Earlier landmark articles were retained when they established an important clinical or methodological foundation that remained relevant to recent developments. Backward citation searching of major reviews and forward citation tracking of influential original studies were also performed.

Searches used combinations of controlled vocabulary and free-text terms related to gastric cancer and AI. Representative terms included “gastric cancer,” “gastric adenocarcinoma,” “stomach neoplasm,” “artificial intelligence,” “machine learning,” “deep learning,” “neural network,” “radiomics,” “endoscopy,” “computed tomography,” “PET/CT,” “digital pathology,” “whole-slide image,” “multimodal,” “foundation model,” “prognosis,” “treatment response,” “immunotherapy,” “surgery,” and “clinical decision support.”

Eligible publications included peer-reviewed original clinical studies, prospective or retrospective validation studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, clinical guidelines, methodological reporting guidelines, and regulatory documents relevant to AI applications in gastric adenocarcinoma.

Original studies were prioritized when they included multicenter recruitment, prospective evaluation, independent external validation, clinically actionable endpoints, comparison with clinicians or standard care, calibration analysis, decision curve analysis (DCA), or evaluation within a real or simulated clinical workflow. Studies were excluded from the principal synthesis when they did not report gastric cancer results separately, focused exclusively on non-human experiments without a clinical AI application, described an algorithm without patient-level evaluation or a clinically interpretable endpoint, were conference abstracts or non-peer-reviewed preprints, or lacked sufficient methodological information for critical interpretation.

Because of substantial heterogeneity across diagnostic, prognostic, therapeutic, surgical, and implementation studies, a single formal risk-of-bias instrument was not applied to all evidence. Representative studies were instead characterized according to study design, dataset and cohort size, internal and external validation, calibration and clinical-utility assessment, proximity to an actionable workflow, and implementation or patient-outcome evidence. These dimensions inform the qualitative evidence-maturity ratings in Tables 1 and 2. High model discrimination alone was not considered sufficient evidence of clinical maturity. Results were synthesized by stage of care and modality; no new meta-analysis was performed.

sections.title: AI in gastric cancer diagnosis and subtyping

paragraphs.en: The most mature application of AI in gastric cancer is endoscopic assistance.5 This is unsurprising because endoscopy is central to screening, diagnosis, and treatment planning, whereas the visual cues that distinguish inflammation, dysplasia, and early carcinoma are subtle and observer dependent.4 Recent studies have shown that deep learning systems are being developed not only to flag suspicious lesions on white-light imaging but also to classify lesion type, estimate invasion depth, and assist margin delineation using image enhanced modalities such as narrow-band imaging and linked color imaging.25 A 2023 systematic review of AI assisted endoscopy that included 42 original studies further supports this view and showed that deep learning is useful for detection, classification, assessment of invasion depth, margin delineation, segmentation, and early lesion recognition.11

A key translational advance is the shift from static image benchmarking to prospective or near real-time evaluation. In a 2023 endoscopy study, Gong and colleagues developed a deep learning-based clinical decision support system (CDSS) for automated real-time detection and classification of gastric neoplasms.26 In internal testing, the system achieved a 95.6% lesion detection rate, with 89.7% accuracy for four class histologic categorization and 89.2% accuracy for prediction of invasion depth. In a prospective multicenter external test using images from five institutions, performance remained 81.5% for four class classification and 86.4% for binary assessment of invasion depth.26 Although the pilot-randomized component did not show a statistically significant difference in lesion detection during screening, the value of the study lies less in peak accuracy than in demonstrating that AI for gastric endoscopy can be evaluated prospectively across institutions.

The field is shifting from a comparison between AI and the endoscopist toward a more realistic collaborative model in which AI supports the endoscopist.27 A 2023 study reported that AI-assisted interpretation improved the assessment of invasion depth in early gastric cancer.28 This is an actionable endpoint because the depth of invasion strongly influences the appropriateness of endoscopic resection.29 External validation in non-Japanese populations is also increasing. For example, a 2023 Singapore-based study evaluated an AI endoscopic system in a distinct population, underscoring that cross-country testing is both feasible and necessary to reduce geographic overfitting.27 High benchmark performance in a single country dataset is no longer sufficient. Clinical adoption will require robustness to shifts in the lesion spectrum, imaging practice, and background mucosal patterns.30

Image-enhanced endoscopy represents another promising direction.31 A 2024 study reported that linked color imaging combined with computer-aided detection improved gastric cancer detection relative to standard approaches, highlighting that performance depends not only on model architecture but also on the diagnostic quality and disease contrast of the input signal.32 Clinically useful systems will likely be more aware of sequence and context than systems that rely only on individual frames.26

The principal limitations of endoscopic AI remain retrospective image enrichment, inconsistent patient-level splitting, limited multinational evaluation, and insufficient measurement of false-alert burden and workflow benefit. Future trials should compare endoscopists with and without AI under realistic lesion prevalence and should report per-patient sensitivity, unnecessary biopsy rates, procedure time, subgroup performance, and clinically important missed lesions. As summarized in Table 1, endoscopic AI is currently the most translationally mature imaging-related application in gastric cancer, whereas imaging-based staging models remain clinically promising but methodologically less mature.

sections.title: Imaging AI for staging and metastatic risk

paragraphs.en: Cross-sectional imaging is central to gastric cancer staging, assessment of resectability, detection of metastatic disease, treatment planning, and response evaluation.16 Conventional interpretation may, nevertheless, be limited by subtle serosal invasion, small-volume nodal disease, and occult peritoneal dissemination. AI approaches include handcrafted radiomics, deep learning feature extraction, end-to-end image models, and multimodal fusion of imaging with clinical or endoscopic information.

Peritoneal metastasis prediction is among the most extensively studied imaging applications. A 2023 meta-analysis of 10 studies involving 6,199 patients reported a pooled sensitivity of 0.77, specificity of 0.88, and AUC of 0.89 for radiomics-based prediction of peritoneal metastasis.14 These results suggest clinically relevant signal, but heterogeneity was substantial at I2 = 88%, probably reflecting differences in the scanner type, contrast timing, image reconstruction, tumor segmentation, feature selection, reference standards, and patient selection.

Individual PET/CT and CT studies have reported stronger performance in selected cohorts. A PET/CT-based multimodal fusion model integrating radiomic and clinical features achieved AUCs of 0.942 in the training cohort and 0.908 in the testing cohort for preoperative peritoneal metastasis prediction.15 A 2025 CT-radiomics study extracted 1,316 features from tumor and peritumoral regions and reported AUCs of 0.943 and 0.835 in its training and testing cohorts, respectively.33 The decline between development and testing illustrates why internal estimates should not be interpreted as the expected clinical performance.

Imaging AI is also moving beyond single-modality radiomics. A 2025 study involving 691 patients integrated venous-phase CT and endoscopic images for preoperative pathological staging.8 The integrated model achieved a test-set AUC of 0.933, with a sensitivity of 0.869 and specificity of 0.840, and outperformed the individual CT and endoscopic models. This supports the rationale for combining complementary information on mural invasion and mucosal appearance, although the study remained retrospective and lacked geographic external validation.

Other imaging applications include prediction of lymph-node metastasis, peritoneal recurrence, treatment response, nutritional risk, and postoperative outcomes.8 MRI-specific AI evidence in gastric cancer remains comparatively sparse and should not be considered equivalent in maturity to CT or PET/CT. Future studies should use harmonized acquisition protocols, automated quality control and segmentation, independent geographic test cohorts, prespecified clinical thresholds, and direct comparison with conventional staging. Clinical usefulness should be demonstrated through decisions such as staging laparoscopy, neoadjuvant treatment, surgical planning, or surveillance intensity, rather than through AUC alone.

Digital pathology has rapidly advanced from basic tumor segmentation to clinically actionable classification and inference.34 In gastric cancer, this shift is particularly important because routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides contain far more information than is typically extracted in standard practice, including signals related to differentiation, stromal architecture, immune infiltration, vascular invasion, and, in some cases, molecular subtype.35 Pathology AI is emerging not only as an efficiency tool but also as a scalable platform for treatment-relevant inference from routine histology.36

An important area of progress is pathology-based prediction of nodal and vascular metastatic risks. In 2024, an interpretable deep learning model trained on H&E whole-slide images from multiple institutions was developed to predict lymph node metastasis in early gastric cancer.37 This is clinically important because decisions about additional surgery after endoscopic resection often depend on the estimated risk of occult nodal disease, whereas existing pathologic criteria remain imperfect.29 Another 2024 study developed an ensemble deep learning model to detect lymphovascular invasion on gastric cancer whole-slide images and reported very high discrimination.38 Together, these studies move pathology AI closer to treatment-escalation support than to passive morphologic assistance. However, their translational value will ultimately depend on whether they provide reproducible, externally validated information beyond established pathologic criteria, rather than merely repackaging familiar morphologic cues in a more complex computational form.29

Another major advance is low-cost inference of molecular phenotypes from routine H&E slides. A 2025 multicenter retrospective study introduced HER2Net, a deep learning model that predicts human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) status directly from H&E whole-slide images.39 The model was trained on 531 slides from 520 patients and achieved an accuracy of 0.9043 in internal testing and 0.8922 in external multicenter testing.39 The modest decline in performance between internal and external testing suggests that this approach extends beyond a single-center proof of concept. These findings do not support replacing confirmatory HER2 testing.17 However, they do support a practical prescreening role that may shorten the turnaround time and reduce unnecessary testing. In the near term, this positions digital pathology more convincingly as a triage and biomarker-enrichment layer than as a wholesale substitute for immunohistochemistry (IHC), in situ hybridization (ISH), or broader molecular assays.34

This principle also applies to other biomarkers. Although the initial demonstration that deep learning can infer microsatellite instability (MSI) directly from gastrointestinal histology predates the 2022–2025 period,40 recent gastric cancer studies continue to refine this concept through multimodal image-feature extraction and nuclear-segmentation frameworks for MSI and tumor mutational burden (TMB) prediction.41 More broadly, AI is making the bridge between morphology and genotype increasingly actionable, as subtle tissue architecture may serve as a cost-efficient proxy for complex molecular states.18 In gastric cancer, this approach may be particularly valuable for MSI, EBV-associated disease, immune-inflamed phenotypes, and resistance-associated signaling states, all of which are relevant to treatment selection and prognosis.42

Finally, digital pathology is beginning to link morphology to treatment response rather than diagnosis alone.43 In 2024, a multicenter study developed a deep learning histopathology biomarker—ICIsRS—from whole-slide images to predict response to first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer.19 Using 313 whole-slide images from 264 patients and 148,181 image patches, the ensemble model achieved AUCs of 0.92, 0.95, 0.96, and 1.00 across four testing datasets.19 The key point is not the peak AUCs themselves but the finding that routine H&E slides may encode reproducible, treatment-relevant information across datasets.34 Even after accounting for the optimism that can arise in retrospective image-based studies, this remains one of the clearest recent indications that standard pathology slides may contain clinically exploitable predictors of immunotherapy benefit.13 However, the central translational question is whether such models can provide stable added value beyond pathologist assessment, standard biomarkers, and existing treatment-selection frameworks.42 As summarized the most convincing near-term role of digital pathology AI is to support triage, case prioritization, and biomarker enrichment, rather than to replace molecular assays or clinician judgment.

The recent biomarker literature illustrates different levels of translational readiness. HER2Net was developed from 531 slides obtained from 520 patients and achieved accuracies of 0.9043 internally and 0.8922 in external multicenter testing.39 This supports a potential prescreening role, particularly for prioritizing slides or tissue blocks for confirmatory HER2 testing. However, fixation, staining, scanner platforms, tumor heterogeneity, and reference standards remain important sources of error.

Treatment-response models require more cautious interpretation. The ICIsRS model used 313 whole-slide images from 264 patients and reported AUCs of 0.92, 0.95, 0.96, and 1.00 across four testing datasets for prediction of response to first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy.19 Although encouraging, unusually high retrospective performance may reflect selected cohorts, limited event numbers, patch-level sampling, or unmeasured clinical confounding. Prospective studies should determine whether pathology-based enrichment improves treatment allocation beyond established biomarkers such as PD-L1-combined positive score, MSI status, EBV status, HER2, and claudin 18.2 (CLDN18.2).

The most defensible near-term use is, therefore, a layered workflow in which AI identifies suspicious tissue, prioritizes cases, estimates biomarker probability, and selects representative regions for confirmatory testing. Final treatment decisions should remain based on validated assays and multidisciplinary interpretation. This positioning may reduce workload and testing inefficiency without prematurely replacing the molecular or immunohistochemical standards.

This translational logic is illustrated in Figure 2, which shows how pathology AI is currently better positioned as a triage and biomarker-enrichment layer than as a replacement for molecular assays or clinician judgment.

sections.title: AI in prognostic prediction and risk assessment
Spatial biology, single-cell integration, and multi-omics

paragraphs.en: The prognostic frontier in gastric cancer is increasingly spatially informed,44,45 but the available technologies currently serve two distinct translational roles. Spatial pathology AI converts routine or multiplex tissue images into prognostic representations that can be incorporated into existing diagnostic workflows, whereas single-cell, spatial transcriptomic, and broader multi-omics approaches mainly function as upstream discovery platforms for identifying biologically grounded features.43,46 This distinction separates near-term clinical deployment from mechanism-oriented feature discovery without implying that the two approaches are independent.

A pathology-native example is a 2022 NPJ Precision Oncology study that converted multiplex IHC images from 172 patients into cell-graph representations and used graph neural networks to predict survival.47 The “cell-graph signature” achieved a binary survival AUC of 0.960 ± 0.010 and a ternary C-index of 0.823, outperforming the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) 8th edition TNM staging system.48 Beyond performance, the study reframed prognosis as a network property shaped by cell-cell relationships, local immune architecture, and stromal organization, which may capture invasive-front structure and immune exclusion that conventional staging does not fully represent.21,49,50,51,52

A second clinically scalable direction is virtual biomarker generation.53 In 2024, a multimodal attention-based system inferred seven prognostically relevant immune markers from non-antibody-stained fluorescence images and produced prognostic stratification comparable to conventional multiplex immunofluorescence.53 By recovering high-value immune information from a simpler input, this approach illustrates how AI may retain spatial prognostic value while reducing laboratory cost and workflow burden.54

Single-cell and spatial transcriptomic studies complement these deployable approaches by resolving malignant cell states, immune ecotypes, stromal programs, and localized signaling niches associated with recurrence, treatment resistance, and survival heterogeneity.55 Their present value is primarily upstream; they identify mechanism-linked features such as immunosuppressive myeloid states, exhausted T cell niches, invasive epithelial programs, and neutrophil-associated resistance signals that can subsequently be projected into scalable pathology or imaging models.56 Multi-omics integration extends this discovery layer by linking transcriptomic, proteomic, genomic, and clinicopathologic variables to latent axes such as immune activation, stromal dominance, proliferative drive, and metabolic adaptation.57

Accordingly, high-resolution omics should currently be viewed as a biologic discovery and feature-distillation layer, rather than as a standalone clinical predictor. Their longer-term contribution will depend on whether reproducible signals can be anchored to routine histology, imaging, and longitudinal clinical data, thereby producing prognostic models that are both scalable and mechanistically interpretable.58

Single-modality prediction is increasingly inadequate for a disease as biologically and clinically heterogeneous as gastric cancer.59,60 A patient’s prognosis is shaped not only by the radiologic extent and histologic phenotype but also by the immune architecture, molecular subtype, frailty, treatment intensity, perioperative events, and the timing of response or recurrence.4 For this reason, multimodal AI is becoming less an optional technological upgrade and more a necessary design principle for clinically meaningful risk prediction in precision oncology.7

This transition is already visible in both population-level risk prediction and individualized survival modeling.61 At the population level, a 2025 machine learning model developed from the Korean National Health Insurance Service cohort analyzed more than 10 million screened adults and identified familiar drivers, including age, male sex, Helicobacter pylori infection, smoking, and family history.62 Notably, logistic regression achieved the best performance.62 This finding suggests that in structured screening settings, simpler models may remain highly competitive and may even be preferable when transparency, calibration, and transportability are priorities.44 This is an important corrective in a field that is often biased toward algorithmic complexity. Not every clinically useful model needs to be deep, and, in some settings, the most robust solution may also be the most interpretable.45

At the postoperative level, complication prediction represents another clinically meaningful application.63,64 Recent multicenter studies have shown that machine learning models can predict serious or early complications after radical gastrectomy with stable validation performance. These systems are valuable not only because they identify statistical risk but also because they may inform perioperative counseling, prehabilitation intensity, intensive care unit (ICU) triage, nutritional support planning, and tailored postoperative surveillance.65 In this setting, AI becomes clinically relevant when it changes management intensity, rather than merely generating another abstract probability score.66

In advanced disease, the field is moving toward treatment-linked survival prediction, rather than static baseline risk estimation.21 A 2025 systematic review focused on machine learning for gastric cancer survival prediction reflects the maturation of this field.51 Recent studies have also pointed toward models that integrate pathology, CT radiomics, immune surrogates, and longitudinal treatment variables.52 The key shift is conceptual. Survival models become more clinically meaningful when they are explicitly linked to decision points, continuously updated as new information accrues, and evaluated not only for discrimination but also for calibration, temporal robustness, and practical utility.67 Prognostic AI will be most clinically useful when it becomes dynamic, treatment aware, and longitudinally updated. As summarized in Table 2, prognostic modeling in gastric cancer is shifting from static, single-modality prediction toward spatially informed and dynamic multimodal risk stratification. Figure 3 summarizes this paradigm shift from static baseline prediction toward spatially informed and dynamic multimodal risk stratification.

sections.title: AI in treatment decision-making and personalized therapy
Treatment response prediction and regimen optimization

paragraphs.en: A central clinical application of AI in gastric cancer is treatment allocation, rather than diagnosis alone.22 This is particularly relevant in gastric cancer because systemic treatment increasingly includes biomarker-linked options such as HER2-targeted therapy, PD-1 inhibitors, and combination regimens, whereas response heterogeneity remains substantial.68 In this setting, the most clinically valuable AI systems are not simply prognostic models. They are treatment-specific predictors that help identify which patients are most likely to be benefited from a particular therapeutic strategy.69

Digital pathology-based immunotherapy prediction is among the strongest recent developments in this area.19 In a 2024 multicenter study, a histopathology biomarker derived from whole-slide images was developed from 313 whole-slide images obtained from 264 patients, with 148,181 image patches used for model construction.19 The ensemble model achieved AUCs of 0.92, 0.95, 0.96, and 1.00 across four testing datasets for predicting response to first-line PD-1 blockade plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric cancer.19 Complementary studies have also used interpretable machine learning to predict progression-free response duration to sintilimab plus chemotherapy in advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction cancer.70 These studies suggest that even routine laboratory variables can support clinically meaningful response models when analyzed with explainable machine learning approaches.70 These studies place treatment response prediction among the most plausible near-term deployment targets in gastric cancer AI. However, the central methodological challenge is to distinguish a true predictive signal from prognostic enrichment because some models may primarily learn baseline disease severity, rather than treatment-specific benefit.71 Accordingly, future studies should demonstrate that these systems are genuinely predictive rather than merely correlated with overall outcome.72

A second important trend is the estimation of immune contexture from noninvasive data. In 2024, investigators developed a machine learning workflow that used contrast-enhanced CT and clinical variables to predict cluster of differentiation 8 (CD8)-positive T cell infiltration in gastric cancer.73 This is clinically attractive because immune infiltration is prognostic, relevant to treatment response, and difficult to sample repeatedly.73 If robustly validated, radiology-derived immune proxies could function as repeatable whole-tumor biomarkers for treatment selection, treatment monitoring, and potentially adaptive sequencing of systemic therapy.74 Their appeal lies in scalability and repeatability, but their clinical utility will depend on whether they maintain reliable correspondence with biologically meaningful immune states across scanners, institutions, and treatment settings.75

AI may also help optimize upstream prevention strategies related to gastric carcinogenesis. A 2025 Nature Communications study introduced an AI clinician for Helicobacter pylori management based on reinforcement learning.76 The model was trained on 38,049 patients from the European Registry on Helicobacter pylori management. In internal validation, AI-recommended therapies achieved a 94.1% eradication success rate, compared with 88.1% for clinician-prescribed therapies that were not aligned with AI recommendations.76 This represented an absolute improvement of 6.0% and was replicated in an external cohort of 7,186 patients. This is an important development because it extends AI in gastric cancer beyond diagnosis and treatment into carcinogenesis prevention. From a public health perspective, optimized eradication strategies may ultimately have a broader population-level impact than many downstream oncology models. The next practical wave of AI in gastric cancer may, therefore, include prevention-oriented decision support, alongside response stratification and regimen optimization.77 Key treatment-allocation and prevention-oriented studies are summarized.

Compared with diagnostic AI, surgical AI in gastric cancer remains at an earlier stage, but evidence is expanding from retrospective video analysis toward workflow parsing, skill analytics, and patient-specific navigation.78 Most systems still perform foundational perception tasks rather than autonomous guidance, which is an appropriate developmental sequence because reliable recognition of the operative scene is a prerequisite for clinically meaningful intraoperative support.

Concrete evidence is emerging for workflow recognition and skill assessment. A 2024 multicenter study used laparoscopic distal gastrectomy videos from 20 hospitals, annotated the operation into nine phases, and achieved an overall phase-recognition accuracy of 88.8%. Model-derived phase duration and surgical-field development scores also differed between high- and low-skill groups, supporting the automated performance assessment.79 In parallel, automated instrument recognition in robotic distal gastrectomy showed that patterns of instrument use during infrapyloric lymphadenectomy could distinguish more experienced surgeons from less experienced surgeons.80 These systems are most immediately relevant to standardized training analytics, workflow monitoring, and objective feedback, rather than procedural autonomy.

AI-assisted navigation has also entered prospective feasibility testing. In a 30-patient study of robotic distal gastrectomy, patient-specific three-dimensional models reconstructed from preoperative CT angiography reproduced all vessels and vascular variations encountered during surgery, and no system-related intraoperative events were reported.23 Compared with matched controls, the navigation group had numerically shorter anesthesia time (218.6 min vs. 230.3 min), operative time (177.1 min vs. 193.9 min), and console time (129.3 min vs. 147.4 min), although these differences were not statistically significant.23 Earlier three-dimensional angiographic analyses likewise support the feasibility of patient-specific perigastric vascular mapping before gastrectomy.81

These examples remain feasibility studies, rather than evidence of improved patient outcomes. Future studies should, therefore, use prospective multicenter comparisons with predefined endpoints such as navigation error, unintended vascular injury, blood loss, operative and console time, lymph-node yield, conversion, pancreatic fistula, anastomotic leakage, and 30-day morbidity. At present, the most defensible role of surgical AI in gastric cancer is to support perception, navigation, workflow standardization, and training while preserving surgeon oversight.

AI is beginning to influence gastric cancer not only at the level of diagnosis and prognostic assessment but also across the therapeutic development pipeline.82 In this domain, however, the most credible near-term role of AI in gastric cancer is not fully autonomous de novo drug discovery. Instead, its more realistic translational value lies in prioritizing therapeutic hypotheses, optimizing companion diagnostics, enriching biomarker-guided patient selection, and modeling treatment pathways. In gastric cancer, AI is most likely to matter where it improves the matching of therapies to patients within biomarker-defined subgroups.22

A particularly relevant application is biomarker enrichment for existing and emerging targeted therapies and immunotherapy strategies. In gastric cancer, treatment selection increasingly depends on markers such as HER2, fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2), CLDN18.2, and immune phenotypes related to PD-1 and PD-L1.68 These biomarkers are clinically actionable, but their interpretation is often complicated by intratumoral heterogeneity, variable staining intensity, sampling limitations, and differences in scoring and testing workflows.83 This is where AI-enhanced digital pathology and multimodal modeling may add the greatest near-term value. By integrating histomorphology, spatial distribution patterns, immunohistochemical signals, and clinicopathologic context, AI could help identify biomarker-enriched regions, flag borderline or potentially discordant cases, prioritize specimens for confirmatory IHC, ISH, or next-generation sequencing (NGS) testing, and improve screening efficiency for biomarker-defined therapeutic pathways.39 In this sense, AI may strengthen companion diagnostics not by replacing established assays but by making the molecular triage more efficient, more standardized, and more biologically informed.39

This logic is particularly relevant for HER2-directed therapy, where spatial heterogeneity and incomplete sampling can lead to underrecognition of eligible patients.84 It is also relevant for FGFR2-directed strategies, where biologically meaningful subgroups may be small and difficult to identify efficiently. It is equally relevant for CLDN18.2-targeted treatment, where accurate stratification depends not only on positivity but also on the extent and distribution of expression. Similarly, for PD-1-based therapy, AI may help move beyond a single-marker view by integrating morphology, immune contexture, and clinical features to identify patients with a higher probability of being benefited than conventional biomarkers alone can provide. As a result, the most immediate impact of AI in this area may lie less in inventing new drugs and more in improving patient enrichment, reducing missed eligibility, and refining trial matching for therapies that are already clinically or developmentally relevant in gastric cancer.22

A second important opportunity is therapeutic simulation, particularly in the context of treatment sequencing. Gastric cancer management increasingly involves multiple layers of decision-making, including perioperative therapy, first-line systemic treatment, later-line targeted options, and biomarker-driven immunotherapy combinations.85 In this setting, AI could evolve into a decision-support layer that models likely outcomes under different treatment pathways using integrated pathology, imaging, laboratory, molecular, and longitudinal clinical data. This does not yet amount to a fully realized digital twin, and evidence that is specific to gastric cancer is not yet sufficiently mature to support strong clinical claims.86 Even so, the concept remains highly relevant. Rather than treating each therapy choice as an isolated event, AI may help estimate which sequence or combination strategy is most appropriate for a given patient, especially when biomarker overlap, borderline eligibility, or competing treatment priorities complicate decision-making.86 Its most plausible role is to support sequence selection when biomarker overlap, borderline eligibility, or competing priorities complicate treatment choice.

The most defensible near-term role of AI in this domain is to improve companion diagnostics, strengthen patient enrichment, and refine treatment matching rather than to pursue autonomous drug invention.87 Framed in this way, drug discovery and therapeutic simulation become less of a speculative future addition and more of a clinically relevant extension of precision oncology in gastric cancer. Figure 4 summarizes how therapeutic AI in gastric cancer is shifting from retrospective response prediction toward clinically actionable enrichment, companion-diagnostic support, prevention-oriented decision support, and, potentially, future treatment-path simulation.

Despite rapid progress, gastric cancer AI remains fundamentally constrained by heterogeneity in both data generation and disease representation.88 Endoscopy datasets vary according to processor generation, image-enhancement mode, insufflation technique, bowel preparation quality, lesion prevalence, annotation practice, and operator behavior.88 Imaging datasets differ across scanner vendors, contrast protocols, reconstruction parameters, and segmentation workflows. Pathology data are affected by stain variation, scanner settings, section thickness, processing pipelines that are specific to individual institutions, and labeling conventions. These factors are major sources of instability that can inflate retrospective performance and weaken generalizability.66

An additional and often underappreciated issue is label quality. Many gastric cancer AI models, particularly in digital pathology, rely on weak labels such as diagnoses made at the slide level, treatment labels, or outcome labels that may not correspond precisely to the most informative microscopic regions.89 This creates a risk of label noise because models may learn from partially misaligned or biologically diluted supervision, rather than from signals that are truly specific to the lesion. In pathology, this problem is especially relevant when only biomarker status or response outcomes are available at the case level, which forces algorithms to infer regional importance indirectly.89 Similar concerns apply in imaging studies when radiologic endpoints are derived from imperfect reference standards or when segmentation boundaries vary substantially across annotators.66

Methodological bias can also arise from data handling itself. In retrospective radiomics and image-based deep learning studies, data leakage remains a recurrent concern, particularly when image splitting is performed at the image, patch, or lesion level rather than strictly at the patient level, or when preprocessing steps inadvertently expose information from the test set.90 Such leakage can lead to overly optimistic estimates of performance that do not survive external validation.66 In addition, class imbalance and prevalence shift are common in gastric cancer AI because early neoplastic lesions, occult metastasis, rare molecular subtypes, and treatment responders may represent only a minority of cases. A model trained in a highly enriched research cohort may, therefore, perform poorly when applied to real-world populations with different disease prevalence, referral patterns, or lesion spectra.

A second major issue is geographic imbalance. Much of the strongest gastric cancer AI literature originates from East Asian cohorts because of the region’s high disease burden, organized screening, and concentrated digital data resources. However, models optimized in high-incidence settings may not transfer directly to lower-incidence populations with different lesion spectra, background gastritis patterns, molecular subtype prevalence, referral pathways, and disease prevalence.85 External studies in Singapore and European Helicobacter pylori cohorts show that cross-regional transfer is feasible, but multinational evaluation under explicit distribution shift remains uncommon.91

Targeted strategies should operate across the data, model, evaluation, and deployment levels. First, international consortia should prospectively collect regionally diverse cohorts, using harmonized acquisition protocols, annotation standards, endpoint definitions, and core metadata on ethnicity, geography, device, operator, and care pathway. Second, development studies should use patient-level splitting and report leave-one-center-out or leave-one-country-out validation, temporal validation, and region-stratified performance, rather than relying only on random internal splits.66,92,93 Third, domain-generalization and transfer learning methods should be combined with privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) or federated benchmarking so that models can be trained or evaluated across institutions without centralizing raw patient data.94 These approaches must still be audited for non-identically distributed data and subgroup-specific failure. Fourth, deployment in a new region should include local recalibration, prespecified threshold selection, uncertainty or out-of-distribution flagging, and continuous monitoring for prevalence and performance drift. Finally, comparative prospective studies should test clinician-alone workflow versus clinician-AI workflow in the target population and report subgroup fairness, calibration, net clinical benefit, and patient- or workflow-level outcomes.91

The geographic distribution of gastric cancer AI research reflects major differences in disease incidence, screening policy, procedural volume, digital infrastructure, and data availability. East Asia contributes much of the strongest evidence because Japan, South Korea, and China combine high case volumes, experienced endoscopists, organized or risk-based screening, and large institutional image repositories. These conditions have supported real-time endoscopic systems, invasion-depth classifiers, radiomics models, digital pathology tools, and surgical-video datasets.

External evaluation outside original development settings remains uncommon. A Singapore-based study demonstrated the feasibility of evaluating a gastric-neoplasia endoscopy model in a population and clinical environment distinct from its Japanese development setting.27 Such studies are essential because lesion prevalence, background mucosal disease, endoscopy practice, and referral patterns may alter performance. Validation in a second Asian country, however, does not, by itself, establish global transportability.

In Europe, registry-based prevention models, digital pathology cohorts, and multimodal analyses are increasingly relevant. The European Registry on Helicobacter pylori management supported the development of an AI clinician for eradication treatment selection,76 while implementation is also shaped by medical-device legislation, data-protection requirements, and the European Union AI Act. In North America, gastric cancer-specific prospective deployment studies remain less common because population-wide endoscopic screening is not routine; much of the evidence derives from tertiary centers, public molecular resources, or pan-cancer pathology frameworks.

Low- and middle-income countries face shortages of endoscopists, pathology specialists, digital scanners, modern processors, stable connectivity, and referral capacity.95 AI may support triage and training, but importing a computationally intensive model trained in a high-resource setting could widen disparities. Priorities should include locally relevant datasets, affordable or offline models, compatibility with existing equipment, workforce training, evaluation under local prevalence, and clear referral pathways. The appropriate system for a high-volume East Asian screening center may, therefore, differ substantially from that required in a rural or resource-constrained hospital.

High discrimination alone is not sufficient for clinical adoption.66 Many gastric cancer AI systems remain black box predictors, and commonly used post-hoc visualization tools such as Grad CAM or SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), although useful for inspection, do not, by themselves, establish causal faithfulness or clinical reliability.96 In high-stakes contexts, such as judging invasion depth, deciding on additional surgery or selecting immunotherapy, clinicians need explanations that are not merely visually persuasive but also biologically coherent, operationally relevant, and auditable within a clinical responsibility framework.66

A useful distinction can be made between attention-based explanation and mechanism-linked explanation. Attention maps indicate where a model appears to focus. By contrast, mechanism-linked explanations connect predictions to recognizable pathobiology, such as stromal remodeling, immune exclusion, vascular invasion, or biomarker-enriched tissue regions. Gastric cancer is particularly well suited to this shift because pathologists and endoscopists already interpret structured morphologic cues in routine practice.66 The more closely the AI explanations align with this domain knowledge, the more likely they are to support clinician trust, meaningful audit, and responsible deployment.97 In practice, explainability will matter only if model representations remain clinically legible and relevant to decision-making.97

However, trust is not determined by explainability alone. Human factor risks must also be considered.98 Even a well-performing model can create automation bias if clinicians begin to rely too heavily on AI suggestions, especially in time-pressured settings such as endoscopy or intraoperative support.98 Conversely, poorly calibrated or poorly integrated tools may be ignored altogether, leading to underuse, even when they are potentially beneficial.98 Repeated low-value alerts may also produce alert fatigue and reduce attention to truly important prompts.99 Over the longer term, overdependence on automated assistance could contribute to deskilling if core interpretive abilities are gradually displaced rather than supported.

For these reasons, clinical acceptance depends not only on whether a model is understandable but also on whether it is introduced in a way that preserves appropriate human oversight.98 Gastric cancer AI systems should, therefore, be designed to support trust calibration rather than blind trust.100 Clinicians should understand when a model is likely to be reliable, when uncertainty is high, and when override or independent review is appropriate. In mature deployment, the most acceptable systems will be those that enhance expert judgment without narrowing clinical vigilance or eroding professional competence.

Most gastric cancer AI studies remain retrospective, and this is the principal limitation on evidence maturity.5 The 2023 real-time endoscopy CDSS is notable because it included prospective multicenter external testing, whereas many otherwise high-performing systems remain confined to retrospective datasets.26 Similarly, the radiomics meta-analysis for peritoneal metastasis reported an AUC of 0.89 but a substantial heterogeneity (I2 = 88%).14 These examples show that model availability is no longer the main constraint; the priority is the consistent clinical evaluation.

Several representative studies show why strong discrimination should not be equated with clinical maturity. The peritoneal-metastasis radiomics meta-analysis reported an AUC of 0.89 but a heterogeneity (I2) of 88%.14 In the real-time endoscopy CDSS, four-class accuracy declined from 89.7% internally to 81.5% in multicenter external testing.32 HER2Net declined from 0.9043 internal accuracy to 0.8922 external accuracy,53 while the ICIsRS model reported retrospective AUCs as high as 1.00 without prospective treatment-allocation evidence.19 In a national cohort of more than 10 million screened adults, logistic regression outperformed more complex machine learning approaches.62 These examples support external validation, calibration, realistic prevalence, and comparison with simpler models and standard practice.

Clinical evaluation should be reported in a standardized, task-appropriate framework. For detection and classification, studies should report sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive values (PPVs and NPVs, respectively), AUCs, and performance at prespecified operating thresholds, with per-patient and per-lesion results where relevant. For time-to-event prediction, the C-index and time-dependent AUCs should be accompanied by calibration plots, calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, and Brier score. Across all tasks, discrimination should be complemented by decision-curve net benefit, comparison with the established clinical models and clinician performance, and the workflow outcomes such as examination time, alert burden, missed-lesion rate, treatment reclassification, complications, or patient outcomes. Robustness reporting should include geographic, temporal, device, operator, and clinically relevant subgroup analyses.93

A clinically credible evidence pathway should progress from patient-level internal validation to external geographic and temporal validation, followed by silent prospective testing, comparative or interventional workflow evaluation, and post-deployment surveillance.93 Each stage should have a predefined deployment claim, locked or tightly governed model updates, and explicit criteria for acceptable calibration, subgroup performance, and clinical utility. This staged approach helps distinguish an academically strong model from a system that is ready to influence care.

Regulatory challenges compound the evidentiary problem. Adaptive or multimodal systems that actively support decisions require clearer controls for data provenance, model updates, human oversight, cybersecurity, and post-deployment monitoring than static triage tools. Real-world adoption also depends on reimbursement and medicolegal responsibility; even a well-validated system may not diffuse if institutions lack a payment pathway, implementation resources, or agreement on accountability when AI-assisted recommendations contribute to error.101

Accordingly, evidence standards should prioritize calibration, clinical net benefit, usability, fairness, economic feasibility, and accountability, in addition to technical accuracy.101 The central translational question is not whether an algorithm performs well retrospectively, but whether a clearly defined AI-assisted workflow improves decisions or outcomes safely in the intended population. Figure 5 summarizes this evidence pathway.

Clinical implementation should begin with a clearly defined intended use. The same algorithm requires different evidence and workflow designs depending on whether it functions as a second reader, triage tool, diagnostic classifier, risk calculator, or treatment recommendation system. Deployment should specify when the model is activated, which data are required, what output is generated, which clinician receives the output, and what action is expected.

Real-time endoscopic AI requires direct integration with the endoscopy video stream and sufficiently low latency to permit immediate reinspection. Alert presentation must balance sensitivity against distraction and false-positive burden. Systems should record whether alerts were reviewed, accepted, or overridden and should maintain a clear fallback workflow when AI is unavailable.

Imaging AI should be embedded within picture-archiving and communication systems (PACSs), rather than requiring manual export to a separate platform. Digital pathology AI should similarly integrate with whole-slide viewers, laboratory information systems (LISs), and pathology reporting. Multimodal models require standardized data definitions, units, acquisition times, and missing-data handling across hospital information systems (HISs) and electronic health records (EHRs). Deployed systems should maintain model-version records, audit trails, access controls, cybersecurity safeguards, and downtime procedures. Silent prospective deployment can identify integration failures before predictions influence care.

sections.title: Clinician training, human factors, and adoption

paragraphs.en: Clinician adoption cannot be inferred from technical performance alone. Before deployment, endoscopists, radiologists, pathologists, surgeons, nurses, and information-technology personnel should receive role-specific training on intended use, operating thresholds, known failure modes, uncertainty, escalation procedures, and circumstances in which the model should not be used.

Human-AI interaction should be evaluated directly because a model may improve some clinicians, while distracting or misleading others. Studies should compare clinicians with and without AI and report disagreement patterns, override rates, alert burden, interpretation time, and automation-related errors. Institutions should designate clinical and technical owners and regularly review errors, near misses, subgroup performance, user feedback, and drift.

sections.title: Regulation, model updating, and medico-legal responsibility

paragraphs.en: Regulatory requirements depend on intended use, autonomy, and risk. In the United States, AI-enabled medical devices may be evaluated through 510(k), de novo, or premarket approval pathways. FDA guidance permits a predetermined change control plan to describe anticipated modifications, validation procedures, and impact assessments before controlled updates are implemented. In the European Union, medical AI may be governed by medical-device legislation, together with the high-risk requirements of the AI Act, including risk management, data quality, transparency, human oversight, robustness, and post-market monitoring.

Responsibility should not be assigned solely to the clinician who views an AI output. Developers are responsible for design, documentation, validation, and controlled updating; healthcare institutions are responsible for local validation, integration, training, access control, and monitoring; clinical departments should define appropriate-use and escalation pathways; and clinicians remain responsible for interpreting outputs in the context of the individual patient. Institutions should establish procedures for documenting AI-assisted decisions, reporting adverse events, investigating systematic errors, and suspending a model when performance deteriorates.

Scenario 1: During gastroscopy, an AI system highlights a subtle mucosal abnormality. The endoscopist re-examines the area with white-light and image-enhanced imaging and decides whether biopsy or surveillance is appropriate. The AI prompts additional inspection but does not establish the diagnosis. Relevant outcomes include the miss rate, unnecessary biopsy rate, procedure time, and performance across experience levels.

Scenario 2: After a gastric cancer biopsy is scanned, a pathology model estimates the probability of HER2 positivity, MSI, or another treatment-relevant phenotype and identifies representative tumor regions. High-probability or uncertain cases are prioritized for confirmatory IHC, ISH, or molecular testing. Evaluation should include the turnaround time, missed eligible patients, safely deprioritized tests, and cost per correctly identified biomarker-positive patient.

Scenario 3: A CT model identifies a high probability of occult peritoneal metastasis despite the absence of definite radiologic nodules. The result is reviewed at a multidisciplinary meeting, together with conventional staging, and may prompt staging laparoscopy before definitive surgery. The clinically relevant endpoint is whether model-informed assessment reduces non-therapeutic surgery without causing excessive invasive testing.

sections.title: Future perspectives: integration, trustworthiness, and equity
Multimodal foundation models and generalist clinical AI

paragraphs.en: A plausible next phase is the broader use of foundation models and multimodal learning, but their clinical value remains conditional.20 Recent advances in pathology pretraining and biomedical vision language modeling suggest that large, pretrained backbones may support multiple downstream tasks more efficiently than separate models trained from scratch for each application. In gastric cancer, this raises an important possibility. Tasks such as lesion detection, HER2-related prescreening, survival estimation, and treatment response stratification may increasingly be built on shared pretrained representations with task-specific adaptation, rather than on isolated single-purpose models.26

Even so, this possibility should not be overstated. The practical value of foundation models lies less in being universal solvers than in improving label efficiency, transferability, and cross-modal alignment, particularly in clinically fragmented data environments.101 Clinically, the most useful systems are likely to be oriented toward multidisciplinary teams and constrained to specific tasks, rather than being fully general.6 Because gastric cancer management is inherently multidisciplinary, an AI assistant that synthesizes lesion appearance, imaging stage, pathologic risk, biomarker probability, and patient frailty is a more realistic near-term goal than a fully general clinical agent with open-ended functions.102

Whether such systems become clinically meaningful will depend on more than model size; their outputs must be calibrated, responsive to uncertainty, and aligned with real decision points, rather than merely appearing technically impressive in retrospective benchmarks.45 In practice, multimodal foundation models will matter only if they improve decision quality under prospective evaluation at the workflow level. Accordingly, the most defensible expectation is not that larger models will automatically transform care but that carefully governed multimodal backbones may become useful infrastructure for selected clinical tasks if domain adaptation, interpretability, and deployment governance are handled well.13

sections.title: Deeply embedded explainable and mechanism-aware AI

paragraphs.en: A likely next step is the gradual incorporation of more mechanistic structure into clinically relevant models.47 In gastric cancer, recent work suggests that this transition is feasible. Cell graph survival models, virtual multiplex immune phenotyping, and explainable treatment response systems all move beyond black box pattern recognition toward representations that are more closely tied to tissue biology.19 These developments do not yet establish a new standard of care, but they indicate that the mechanistic structure can increasingly be incorporated into predictive models.

The value of this shift extends beyond clinician trust. Models built around biologically meaningful intermediate states, such as immune exclusion patterns, stromal organization, invasive front architecture, or spatial ecologies that are relevant to treatment, may prove less brittle than systems relying heavily on image statistics that are specific to a given site or on incidental correlations.50 This is particularly relevant in gastric cancer, where morphologic variability across scanners, institutions, and populations can be substantial.24 If biologically anchored abstractions are reproducible across settings, they may support better transportability and more stable external performance than models optimized mainly for internal benchmark accuracy.103

At the same time, AI that is designed to be mechanism aware should not be framed as an automatic solution to generalizability or trust.96 Its advantages will depend on whether the proposed biologic intermediates are reproducible, measurable across datasets, and meaningfully connected to clinical decisions.104 In that sense, the near-term goal is not to replace conventional predictive models with fully mechanistic systems but to progressively incorporate more biologically legible structure into models that are already clinically relevant. In gastric cancer, the most clinically valuable systems may be those that are both accurate and biologically legible.96

If implemented carefully, AI may help reduce inequities in gastric cancer care, particularly by extending decision support to settings with limited specialist resources.105 Risk models developed from routine structured data, affordable pathology prescreening for molecular markers, and noninvasive imaging surrogates for immune contexture could all help broaden access to more stratified care.62 In gastric cancer, this is important because disease burden is unevenly distributed, and access to expert endoscopy, molecular profiling, and subspecialty pathology remains uneven across regions and institutions.2

The most realistic gains in this area are likely to come from scalable triage, prevention-focused support, and biomarker prioritization that is sensitive to resource constraints, rather than from highly sophisticated fully integrated platforms.105 In other words, the most transformative AI applications may not be the most technically complex, but rather the ones that improve access to high-quality decision-making at scale.106 This makes prevention and early risk stratification especially important. When AI supports Helicobacter pylori management, screening prioritization, or affordable enrichment for confirmatory testing, its impact on public health may exceed that of some later-stage oncology tools, provided that these systems remain usable in settings with fewer resources.76

A more distant possibility is the development of practical digital twins for gastric cancer. These would be patient-specific computational models that estimate likely outcomes under different treatment strategies using multimodal longitudinal data.107 However, this should still be viewed as a conditional and relatively distant objective, rather than an imminent clinical reality. At present, the evidence base does not support routine digital twinning in gastric cancer, and several prerequisites remain underdeveloped. These include stable longitudinal data capture, reliable multimodal integration, validated updating of treatment response, and governance frameworks for iterative decision support. For now, digital twins should be regarded as a conditional long-term objective rather than a near-term clinical reality.108,109

Evidence reviewed here supports five immediate priorities for gastric cancer AI. First, future studies should progress from single-center retrospective development to prospective, multicenter, and multiregional evaluation. Second, discrimination should be reported together with calibration, prespecified threshold performance, decision-curve net benefit, and clinically relevant subgroup results. Third, AI-assisted care should be compared directly with existing workflows and with clinician performance without AI. Fourth, trials should evaluate workflow efficiency, safety, resource use, cost effectiveness, and patient-level outcomes, rather than model accuracy alone. Fifth, deployment should include local validation, version control, uncertainty management, post-market surveillance, and predefined responsibility for errors and model updates.

Across domains, priority should shift from additional retrospective model development to prospective, comparative evaluation of clearly defined AI-assisted workflows. Multiregional validation, standardized metrics, local calibration, and monitoring under distribution shift will determine whether apparently strong models deliver reproducible clinical benefit. If these requirements are met, gastric cancer could become a leading example of AI progressing from retrospective pattern recognition to clinically accountable precision medicine.
